connectShopifyStore.title: How to connect your Shopify store
connectShopifyStore.body:
To start using DisputeDesk, you need to connect your Shopify store. Here's how:

1. From the portal dashboard, click "Connect store" in the setup checklist (or use the sidebar link).
2. Enter your store's domain (e.g. my-store.myshopify.com).
3. You'll be redirected to Shopify to authorize DisputeDesk.
4. Grant the requested permissions — DisputeDesk needs access to orders, disputes, dispute evidence, fulfillments, and customer data.
5. Once authorized, you'll land on your dashboard with the connected store already active. The setup checklist will advance to the next step.

To switch between stores, click the store name in the sidebar to open the store selector. You can connect additional stores from that page.

Reconnecting a store:
If DisputeDesk has been updated with new permissions (e.g. after an app update), you may need to reconnect your store to grant the latest permissions. On the store selector page, click the "Reconnect (refresh permissions)" link below your store name. You'll be redirected to Shopify to re-authorize. Your existing data and settings are preserved — only the permissions are refreshed.

Clear shop & reconnect: In the portal sidebar, under the store name, you'll see a "Clear shop & reconnect" link. Use this if the current shop context is stuck or you want to disconnect and connect again from scratch. It clears your selected shop and sends you to the connect store page; you stay signed in with your portal account.

Your store data is encrypted and never shared with third parties.

After connecting, DisputeDesk will automatically sync your open disputes. This usually takes a few seconds.

shopifyAppStoreInstall.title: Installing from the Shopify App Store
shopifyAppStoreInstall.body:
DisputeDesk is available on the Shopify App Store. That is the recommended way to add the app to a store.

From the App Store:
1. Go to the Shopify App Store (apps.shopify.com) and search for DisputeDesk.
2. Click Add app and choose which store to install on.
3. Review and approve the permissions Shopify shows. DisputeDesk needs access to orders, disputes, dispute evidence, fulfillments, and related store data to build evidence packs.
4. After installation, open Shopify Admin, then Apps, then DisputeDesk to use the embedded app.

From our website:
If you started on disputedesk.app or another marketing page, follow the sign-up or install prompts. You will still complete Shopify OAuth. Then open DisputeDesk from Apps in Admin for billing, saving evidence, and the full embedded experience.

Tip: Opening the app from Shopify Admin (Apps, then DisputeDesk) keeps your store session reliable. If you see connection or billing errors, try Clear shop & reconnect in the portal sidebar or reopen the app from Admin. See also "Can't upgrade: Store session is invalid" in Help.

Next: read "Your first dispute sync" and "Understanding the dashboard."

understandingDashboard.title: Understanding the dashboard
understandingDashboard.body:
The dashboard gives you an at-a-glance overview of your dispute operations.

Key metrics displayed:
- Open Disputes: chargebacks currently awaiting a response.
- Win Rate: percentage of disputes resolved in your favor.
- Auto-Saved: evidence packs automatically saved to Shopify this month.
- Resolved: total disputes closed (won or lost).

The Automation Status card shows your current settings: whether auto-build and auto-save are enabled, the minimum completeness score, and whether the blocker gate is active.

The Recent Disputes table lists your latest chargebacks. The Order column links directly to the order in your Shopify Admin. Click View Details on any row to see full dispute details and manage evidence.

firstDisputeSync.title: Your first dispute sync
firstDisputeSync.body:
After connecting your store, DisputeDesk syncs your open disputes automatically.

How syncing works:
- DisputeDesk checks Shopify for new and updated disputes via the Shopify GraphQL API.
- Disputes are imported with their reason, amount, status, due date, and linked order information.
- Syncing happens automatically via webhooks when Shopify notifies us of changes.
- You can also trigger a manual sync by clicking "Sync Now" on the Disputes page.

After the first sync, if you have automation enabled, DisputeDesk will start evaluating rules and building evidence packs automatically for any disputes that need a response.

automationOverview.title: How automation works
automationOverview.body:
DisputeDesk is automation-first. Here's the flow:

1. A new dispute appears in Shopify.
2. DisputeDesk detects it (via webhook or scheduled sync).
3. Your rules are evaluated to decide: auto-pack or send to review queue.
4. If auto-pack: an evidence pack is built automatically from your order data, tracking info, and store policies.
5. The completeness score is calculated. If it meets your threshold and there are no blockers, the evidence is saved to Shopify automatically.
6. If review is required: the pack appears in your Review Queue for manual approval.

**Pack library vs routing rules:** Templates you install under Packs live in your evidence library (sections and narratives you can edit). **Automation rules** only decide whether a new dispute runs the standard auto-build pipeline or is sent to the review queue first—they do not select a library template for that automated build. Auto-build uses order, tracking, and policy collectors.

You control every step through your automation settings and rules. Automation can be fully enabled, partially enabled (auto-build but manual save), or disabled entirely.

**New dispute email (review mode):** When a dispute is routed to review and a pack build is queued, the “ready to review” email is only sent after automated evidence is collected and the pack is ready—not the moment the dispute is first detected. If a build is not started (for example, auto-build is off or you are over your pack limit), you may still be notified at detection time. Turn emails on or off in Settings → Notifications (new dispute alerts).

viewingFilteringDisputes.title: Viewing and filtering disputes
viewingFilteringDisputes.body:
The Disputes page shows all your chargebacks in a sortable table.

You can filter by:
- Status: Needs response, Under review, Won, Lost.
- Search: type keywords to find specific disputes by ID, order number, or reason.

The table shows each dispute's ID, linked order, amount, reason, status, deadline, and when it was last synced.

Two tabs are available:
- All Disputes: every dispute regardless of status.
- Review Queue: only disputes flagged for manual review (based on your rules).

Click any dispute row to open the detail page where you can view evidence packs, generate new packs, or re-sync from Shopify.

disputeDetailPage.title: Dispute detail page
disputeDetailPage.body:
Open any dispute from the list to see the full detail view.

What you see:
- KPI strip: amount, status, due date, and time remaining.
- Managed by DisputeDesk: the chargeback workflow is prepared in this app.
- Dispute status: a five-step overview (Created → Pack → Saved → Review → Outcome). Steps update as evidence packs are built and saved to Shopify; terminal dispute statuses (for example won or lost) mark every step complete.
- Customer and order: profile and order data from Shopify, with links where available.
- Supplemental evidence: after at least one pack has been saved to Shopify (manually or by automation), use Open evidence pack to add extra supporting files on the pack page. Until then, the section explains that uploads unlock after a save to Shopify.
- Timeline: recent Shopify order events plus DisputeDesk events (such as when evidence was saved).
- Evidence packs: all packs for this dispute with completeness, blockers, and links.

Use Generate Pack to create packs, Re-sync to refresh from Shopify, and Open dispute in Shopify when you need Admin. If you change the app locale, timeline messages may follow the store language where Shopify returns localized order events.

syncingDisputes.title: Syncing disputes from Shopify
syncingDisputes.body:
DisputeDesk keeps your disputes up to date through two mechanisms:

1. Webhooks: Shopify sends real-time notifications when disputes are created or updated. DisputeDesk processes these instantly.
2. Manual sync: Click "Sync Now" on the Disputes page to trigger an immediate sync. This is useful if you suspect a webhook was missed.

During a sync, DisputeDesk:
- Fetches all open disputes from Shopify.
- Creates new records for any disputes not yet tracked.
- Updates existing disputes with the latest status and information.
- For new disputes, evaluates your rules and triggers automation if applicable.

Sync status is shown with a "Last synced" timestamp on each dispute.

reviewQueue.title: The review queue
reviewQueue.body:
The Review Queue contains disputes that require your manual review before evidence is saved to Shopify.

Disputes end up in the review queue when:
- A rule routes them to review (e.g. high-value disputes over a certain amount).
- No rule matches and the default action is review.
- You have "Require review before auto-save" enabled in your automation settings.

From the Review Queue tab on the Disputes page, you can:
- See all disputes awaiting your attention.
- Click into any dispute to review the evidence pack.
- Click "Approve" to trigger the automation pipeline (pack building and saving).

This gives you full control over which disputes get automated responses and which ones you want to handle personally.

approvingDisputes.title: Approving disputes from the review queue
approvingDisputes.body:
When a dispute is in your Review Queue, you need to approve it before DisputeDesk will build and save evidence.

To approve a dispute:
1. Go to the Disputes page and switch to the "Review Queue" tab.
2. Click the "Approve" button next to the dispute.
3. DisputeDesk will immediately trigger the automation pipeline.
4. An evidence pack will be built from your order data, tracking, and policies.
5. If the pack passes your completeness and blocker gates, evidence will be saved to Shopify.

You can also approve from the dispute detail page by clicking "Approve & Save."

All approvals are logged in the audit trail for compliance tracking.

howPacksBuilt.title: How evidence packs are built automatically
howPacksBuilt.body:
When DisputeDesk builds an evidence pack, it automatically collects evidence from multiple sources:

- Order data: line items, amounts, billing address (city-level only — PII is redacted), customer tenure, and refund history.
- Fulfillment & tracking: carrier name, tracking numbers, tracking URLs, and delivery status.
- Store policies: snapshots of your shipping, refund, terms, and cancellation policies.

The pack is structured by dispute reason. For example, a "Product not received" dispute will prioritize shipping and tracking evidence, while a "Fraudulent" dispute will emphasize order and customer verification.

After collection, DisputeDesk calculates a completeness score and identifies any blockers (missing required evidence). You can then upload additional files to strengthen the pack.

**Library pack templates:** Installing a template from the Packs page adds a pack to your **library** for narratives, sections, and editing. That is separate from each **automated per-dispute build**, which uses the collectors pipeline above. The automated build does not currently merge your library template structure into the pack automatically.

generatingPackManually.title: Generating a pack manually
generatingPackManually.body:
You can manually generate an evidence pack for any dispute:

1. Go to the dispute detail page.
2. Click "Generate Pack" (or "Generate New Pack" if a pack already exists).
3. DisputeDesk will collect evidence from your order, tracking, and policy data.
4. The pack will appear on the page once building is complete (usually a few seconds).

Manual generation is useful when:
- Automation is disabled and you want to create packs on demand.
- You want to regenerate a pack after uploading new evidence.
- A previous pack failed and you want to retry.

Note: pack generation counts against your monthly quota. Check your usage on the Billing page.

completenessScore.title: Understanding the completeness score
completenessScore.body:
Every evidence pack has a completeness score from 0% to 100%. This score indicates how much of the recommended evidence has been collected.

How it works:
- Each dispute reason has a template of expected evidence items (e.g. tracking info, delivery proof, policy snapshots).
- DisputeDesk checks which items are present in the pack.
- Required items contribute more weight than optional ones.
- The score is the weighted percentage of collected vs. expected items.

Scoring thresholds:
- 80%+ (green): strong pack, ready for auto-save.
- 60–79% (yellow): acceptable but could be stronger.
- Below 60% (red): weak pack — consider uploading more evidence.

If you have auto-save enabled, packs below your configured minimum score will not be saved automatically. You can adjust this threshold in Settings > Automation.

fixingBlockers.title: Fixing blockers in your evidence pack
fixingBlockers.body:
Blockers are missing required evidence items that prevent an evidence pack from being auto-saved to Shopify.

Common blockers include:
- Missing tracking information for "Product not received" disputes.
- Missing refund policy for "Credit not processed" disputes.
- Missing order details when order data could not be fetched.

To fix blockers:
1. Open the evidence pack from the dispute detail page.
2. Check the "Evidence Checklist" section — blockers are highlighted in red.
3. Upload the missing evidence using the upload section.
4. After uploading, the pack will re-evaluate and update the blocker status.

If you have "Enforce zero blockers" enabled in automation settings, packs with any remaining blockers will not be auto-saved. You can disable this gate if you prefer to save packs even with missing items.

uploadingEvidence.title: Uploading additional evidence
uploadingEvidence.body:
You can upload files to strengthen your evidence pack:

1. Open the evidence pack detail page.
2. Scroll to the "Upload Evidence" section.
3. Click to upload or drag and drop files.
4. Allowed types: PNG, JPG/JPEG, and PDF — the formats Shopify Payments documents for dispute file uploads.
5. Combined size of all supporting uploads on this evidence pack cannot exceed about 4 MB (Shopify's limit for dispute evidence files). Larger single files are rejected automatically, and uploads that would push your pack beyond the combined cap are blocked.

DisputeDesk can attach qualifying files through Shopify Payments where permitted, and may still include secure DisputeDesk links inside the narrative so reviewers can open them. Links expire 180 days after evidence is saved to Shopify.

Common uploads include:
- Screenshots of customer communication.
- Delivery confirmation photos.
- Signed receipts or invoices.
- Additional tracking documentation.

evidenceChecklist.title: Evidence checklist explained
evidenceChecklist.body:
The Evidence Checklist shows what evidence has been collected and what's still missing.

Each item in the checklist is marked as:
- Collected (green check): this evidence has been found and included.
- Required but missing (red, labeled "required"): this is a blocker — you need to provide this evidence.
- Recommended (yellow): not strictly required, but providing it would strengthen your case.

The checklist is tailored to each dispute's reason code. For example:
- Product Not Received: prioritizes tracking, delivery proof, and shipping policy.
- Fraudulent: prioritizes order verification, customer details, and AVS/CVV match.
- Credit Not Processed: prioritizes refund records and refund policy.

Focusing on required items first will improve your completeness score and remove blockers that prevent auto-saving.

evidenceStrengthRubric.title: Evidence strength rubric (Strong / Moderate / Supporting / Invalid)
evidenceStrengthRubric.body:
Each row in your evidence pack carries a strength badge. The badge reflects what the data actually proves to the issuer — not whether the row was collected. **Collected ≠ Strong. Supporting ≠ bad.** Green (Strong) means "this materially improves the likelihood of winning."

**🟢 Strong**
The evidence by itself materially shifts the case in your favor.
1. **Payment authentication (AVS + CVV).** Strong only when AVS matches AND CVV matches. Shows the buyer likely had access to correct billing/card details.
2. **Delivery proof with signature.** Strong when the carrier records a signature (signature_confirmed). Direct proof goods reached the recipient.
3. **Signed agreement or contract.** Strong when a signed customer agreement is uploaded. Shows explicit customer participation.
4. **Account/login activity with clear session consistency.** Strong when the customer logged in, ordered from a consistent device/session/IP, and there's no suspicious mismatch.
5. **Prior undisputed transaction history.** Strong when the same customer/card/email/address has previously ordered successfully without disputes.
6. **Explicit customer communication.** Strong when the customer confirms the purchase, delivery, use, or satisfaction in writing.
7. **Digital access / usage proof.** Strong when the customer accessed, downloaded, activated, logged in, or used the product/service. Especially powerful for digital and service disputes.
8. **Refund / cancellation policy acceptance.** Strong only when the customer explicitly accepted the policy at checkout with a timestamp linking to the order. Plain text disclosure does NOT make it Strong.
9. **Delivery to verified billing or customer address.** Strong when tracking confirms delivery to the billing or verified customer address with no mismatch.

**🟡 Moderate**
Useful, but not decisive on its own.
- AVS matches OR CVV matches, but not both.
- Delivery confirmed without a signature (delivered_confirmed).
- Clean IP / location match (no VPN, proxy, or hosting flags).
- Policy text shown but not explicitly accepted at checkout.
- Customer account exists but no strong session proof.
- Order confirmation email sent.
- Fulfillment/tracking exists but the delivery proof is incomplete.

**⚪ Supporting**
Context that completes the pack but won't move the needle on its own.
- Order record.
- Activity log without decisive session proof.
- Refund / shipping / cancellation policy text.
- Customer info / contact details.
- Manual screenshots and uploaded documents without clear decisive content.
- IP data with partial match or VPN / proxy / hosting uncertainty.

**🔴 Invalid**
Reserved for evidence that is explicitly harmful or unusable. "Invalid" never appears just because the payload is missing.
- AVS and CVV both fail.
- Tracking shows label only, never delivered.
- Delivery to an unrelated address.
- IP impossible / harmfully mismatching.
- Policy not applicable to this dispute type.
- Document does not relate to the order.
- Evidence contradicts the defense.

**How this rubric drives your case strength**

The Overview hero is computed from the per-signal verdicts above:
- **Likely to win** (green): 2 or more Strong signals.
- **Could win** (amber): 1 Strong + at least 1 Moderate, OR 2+ Moderate signals.
- **Needs strengthening** (amber): For Fraudulent / Unauthorized transaction disputes only — Payment authentication (AVS+CVV) is Strong but no other decisive signal is collected. The pack is salvageable; adding delivery confirmation, device/session consistency, or explicit customer confirmation would tip it to Likely to win.
- **Hard to win** (red): No Strong signal AND fewer than 2 Moderate signals.

**Fraud-specific rule:** For FRAUDULENT / Unauthorized transaction disputes, AVS+CVV match is the decisive signal. With AVS+CVV Strong, the case is never shown as red "Hard to win" — it's at minimum "Needs strengthening." Pairing AVS+CVV Strong with delivery confirmation (signature_confirmed or delivered_confirmed), device/session consistency, or customer-confirmed communication tips the case to "Likely to win".

Supporting evidence never elevates the hero, but it strengthens your overall pack and provides context for the issuer. Adding a single Strong signal usually has more impact than adding many Supporting items.

defenseLetterRebuttal.title: Defense letter and automated rebuttal text
defenseLetterRebuttal.body:
On the Evidence tab, **Defense letter** is the draft narrative DisputeDesk attaches when you save evidence to Shopify (together with the structured fields and any secure file links).

**Which disputes use the structured issuer narrative**

For these Shopify reason families, the letter follows a fixed six-part flow: opening (chargeback dispute and reversal request), transaction legitimacy (when payment signals exist), payment verification lines (only for data that is actually in the pack), customer and checkout (when order confirmation exists), device and location (when IP enrichment exists, with neutral wording if the country differs from shipping), and closing (reversal request).

- Fraudulent
- Unrecognized
- Product not received
- Duplicate
- General

**Payment lines**

Authorization and capture sentences appear only when the pack supports them. AVS and CVV lines use the strong match codes only (Y and M respectively); other codes do not produce a generic AVS/CVV sentence, so the letter does not overclaim.

**Which disputes keep a different argument**

Credit not processed, subscription canceled, product unacceptable, and digital disputes keep family-specific arguments (for example refund processed, cancellation timeline, or product conformity) instead of the fraud-style legitimacy template.

**Data source**

The text is built from your evidence pack (order, payment verification, IP check, checklist). It does not expose internal scores, "bank eligible" flags, or raw JSON. After you change evidence or regenerate the pack, regenerate the argument if you need the letter refreshed.

evidencePackTemplates.title: Using evidence pack templates
evidencePackTemplates.body:
The Packs page helps you get started with evidence packs using templates.

When you have no packs yet, you'll see recommended templates — pre-built packs for common dispute types (e.g. Fraudulent, Product Not Received). Each template card has an "Install" button: clicking it creates a new pack from that template for your store. After installing, you're taken to the new pack's detail page; you can also open it anytime from the Packs list. Use "Back to packs" on the pack page to return to the library.

In the embedded app (inside Shopify Admin), Evidence Packs shows these templates in a table with row actions (Activate/Edit/Delete). Use "Start from template" to install templates, then activate draft packs from the table.

Tip: If the Packs page looks blank or you can't install templates, reopen DisputeDesk from Shopify Admin (Apps > DisputeDesk) so the embedded shop session is established. DisputeDesk relies on server-side shop identity (httpOnly cookies + middleware) and can't read it from the browser.

**Template Setup Wizard:** In the portal you can use the Template Setup Wizard (Packs > customize or /portal/packs/customize) to configure a new template in four steps: choose evidence types to collect, set evidence sources (where each type comes from — auto, reusable, or manual), review how automation works and choose auto-submit or email-to-review, and activate. See "Template setup wizard" for details.

"Browse All Templates" opens the full template library so you can preview and install any template. "Create from Scratch" starts an empty pack.

Once you have at least one pack, a short banner may appear suggesting you explore more templates; you can dismiss it or click "Browse Templates" to open the library again.

Templates are a quick way to get evidence packs that match best practices; you can always edit documents and settings after installing.

**Related:** **Automation rules** (Rules page or Setup wizard) control whether new disputes are auto-built or sent to the review queue first. They do not swap in a specific library template for each automated build—see "How automation works" and "How evidence packs are built automatically."

templateSetupWizard.title: Template setup wizard
templateSetupWizard.body:
The Template Setup Wizard (in the portal at Packs > customize, or /portal/packs/customize) walks you through setting up a new evidence template in four steps.

**Step 1 — Choose evidence to collect:** Select which types of evidence this template should gather. Each type is marked Required, Recommended, or Optional, and how it is provided: Auto-collected from Shopify, Set in Policies, or You add manually. For policies (e.g. Refund policy), you'll see whether the policy is already set or "Not set — Add in Policies". You must select all required types before continuing.

**Step 2 — Set evidence sources:** Review where DisputeDesk will get each type of evidence. Each selected type is shown with a clear source: auto (pulled from your store), reusable store document (upload once in Policies; use the Upload button to add or link policies), or added manually per dispute. A summary shows how many types are Automated, Reusable, and Manual.

**Step 3 — Review how automation works:** The wizard explains the flow (dispute appears → pack prepared → ready to review). You choose how submission works: **Auto-submit to Shopify** on the dispute due date, or **Email me to review and submit** so you or your team submit manually. The "Important to know" note updates based on your choice.

**Step 4 — Activate template:** Review a summary (evidence types count, how evidence is provided, dispute type, source). You can **Save as draft** to finish later or **Activate template** to start using it. Both actions return you to the Packs library.

In the **embedded app setup** (Shopify Admin), finishing the Install flow with **Activate** creates the library pack as **ACTIVE** so it appears in the Evidence packs step and the **Automation & review** step alongside activated packs.

The sidebar shows your setup progress and a checklist of the four steps. Use "Back to Evidence Packs" at any time to leave the wizard without saving.

definingStorePolicies.title: Defining your store policies
definingStorePolicies.body:
Store policies are included automatically in evidence packs. DisputeDesk uses them to strengthen your case when responding to chargebacks.

Supported policy types: Terms of Service, Refund Policy, Shipping Policy, Privacy Policy, and Contact Information & Customer Service Policy.

The Policies page (portal) shows a Recommended Store Policies section with template cards. For each policy you can:

1. Use a template: click "Use Template" to open a starter document in your chosen language. Edit the content for your store (placeholders are prefilled where possible). You can copy, download, or click "Save & Apply" to save it as that policy type. Templates are starting points, not legal advice — review with your legal team.

2. Upload your own: if you already have a policy as a PDF or Word file, use "Upload" or "Upload Your Own" for that policy type. Accepted formats are PDF and DOCX, max 10 MB. The file is stored securely and a snapshot is used when building evidence packs.

When a policy is already defined, each row shows Edit, Preview, and Download. Use Edit to change the policy text in the same modal (for policies saved from a template); you can then save your changes with "Save & Apply." If the policy was uploaded as a file, Edit opens the template so you can replace it with editable text.

Clear all policies: To remove every policy for the store and re-review from scratch, use "Clear all policies" (top right when you have at least one policy). After confirming, all policy documents are removed; you can then add them again using templates or uploads.

Policy template language: In Settings (Policy templates section), you choose the language of the policy template text (e.g. English or Deutsch). You can use English even if your interface is in another language. This only affects the text when you open a template; it does not change your UI language.

Each policy row shows whether it's defined or not. Keeping policies up to date improves your evidence quality.

configuringAutomation.title: Dispute routing and automation settings
configuringAutomation.body:
**During setup — Automation & review step**

After you install evidence pack templates (Packs step), the **Automation & review** step explains what happens when a **new** dispute syncs from Shopify:

- **Installed library packs:** One row per template-backed pack (**draft** or **active** — not archived), with **Manual review** or **Automatic** handling. Draft packs appear as soon as you install a template, even before you activate the pack on the Packs page. Status badges distinguish active vs draft.
- **Starting presets:** Manual, Review first, or Automatic (Automatic requires installed templates). Manual is suggested for a safe first setup.
- **Default rule (General):** Fallback when no per-reason override applies — choose handling (Manual, Review first, or Auto-build) and a pack template when relevant.
- **Exceptions by reason:** Optional overrides per Shopify dispute reason (e.g. fraud, product not received), each in its own card.
- **Safeguards:** Switches for high-value review and catch-all review. When active, these **override** the default and per-reason rules when their conditions match.
- **Live summary:** A short recap of your effective choices before you save.

The **Evidence packs** step emphasizes **activated** packs in its summary; the Automation step lists **all** installed template-backed packs so you can set routing for drafts too.

You need at least one **installed** pack template before you can assign templates or use the full Automatic path; the setup screen shows a clear message if packs are missing.

**How routing is evaluated:** Amount safeguards → rule for the dispute reason → default (General) → catch-all safeguards (see technical docs: `pickAutomationAction`).

**After setup — Settings > Automation**

Store-wide toggles: auto-build evidence packs, auto-save evidence to Shopify, require review before auto-save, enforce zero blockers, and minimum completeness score (0–100, default 80) for auto-save.

**Rules page**

For custom rules with drag-and-drop order and amount ranges, use **Rules** after setup. See also "Creating your first rule" and "Rule priority."

creatingFirstRule.title: Creating your first rule
creatingFirstRule.body:
Rules let you control how disputes are routed — either to auto-pack or to the review queue.

To create a rule:
1. Go to the Rules page.
2. Click "Add Rule."
3. Fill in the details:
   - Name: a label for your reference (e.g. "High-value review").
   - Match Reasons: select which dispute reasons this rule applies to (leave empty to match all).
   - Amount range: set a minimum and/or maximum dispute amount.
   - Action: choose "Auto-Pack" (automatic processing) or "Send to Review" (manual queue).
4. Click "Create Rule."

Example: create a rule that sends all disputes over $500 to review:
- Name: "High-value review"
- Min Amount: 500
- Action: Send to Review

**What "Auto-Pack" means:** For a matching dispute, DisputeDesk may run the **standard** evidence collection pipeline when the dispute first syncs. It does **not** mean "use a specific pack template from your library"—those templates are managed under Packs separately.

Rules are available on Starter and Pro plans. Free plan users can upgrade from the Billing page.

rulePriority.title: Rule priority and evaluation order
rulePriority.body:
Rules are evaluated top to bottom. The first rule that matches a dispute wins — no further rules are checked.

How matching works:
- If a rule specifies match reasons, the dispute must have one of those reasons.
- If a rule specifies an amount range, the dispute amount must fall within that range.
- If a rule has no conditions (empty reasons, no amount range), it matches all disputes.

To reorder rules, drag and drop them on the Rules page. Put your most specific rules at the top and catch-all rules at the bottom.

If no rule matches a dispute, it goes to the Review Queue by default.

Tip: create a catch-all "Auto-Pack" rule at the bottom to automate everything, and put specific "Send to Review" rules above it for high-value or unusual disputes.

completenessBlockerGates.title: Completeness and blocker gates
completenessBlockerGates.body:
Gates are quality checks that control whether an evidence pack can be saved to Shopify.

**Automatic save gates** (automation pipeline):

1. Completeness gate: the pack's completeness score must meet your configured minimum threshold (default: 80%). Packs below this score will not be auto-saved.

2. Blocker gate: if "Enforce zero blockers" is enabled, any pack with missing required evidence items will not be auto-saved.

Both gates must pass for auto-save to proceed.

**Manual save safeguards** (Save Evidence button on the pack page):

- Empty packs (0% completeness or status "blocked") cannot be saved at all — a warning is shown and the save is blocked.
- Packs below 80% completeness show a confirmation dialog before saving. You can choose to save anyway or go back and add more evidence.
- Packs still building ("queued" or "building" status) show a spinner instead of the save button — wait until building completes.

If a gate or safeguard blocks you:
- Upload additional evidence to improve the score.
- Adjust your gate thresholds in Settings > Automation.
- For manual saves below 80%, confirm the dialog if you're satisfied with what you have.

rulePresets.title: Rule presets and suggested rules
rulePresets.body:
DisputeDesk ships four **suggested starter rules** (fraud, product not received, high-value amount, catch-all). They match the definitions in the product (`lib/rules/presets.ts`).

**Embedded app (Shopify Admin) — Rules**

The Rules screen shows **Automate Your Dispute Workflow** with those four rows. Each row has a **Routing** control: **Auto-Pack** or **Send to Review**. Click **Save starter rules** to create or update the matching rules in your store. Above that, if you have any **ACTIVE** evidence packs in your library, they are listed for context (same data as the Packs page).

**Portal — Rules**

When you have no rules (and your plan supports rules), you may see an empty state with preset cards and **Install Suggested Rules** to add all at once. Presets are idempotent: installing again won't create duplicates.

**Setup wizard**

The **Automation & review** step uses the richer per-reason + safeguards flow (see "Dispute routing and automation settings") and lists **every installed template-backed library pack** (draft or active) for per-pack handling. The embedded Rules starter list is a faster path to the same four presets with two actions each.

Rules are evaluated in priority order (portal: reorder on the Rules page). Rule presets are a good starting point; you can edit or delete any rule after installation. Rules require a Starter or Pro plan.

planComparison.title: Comparing Free, Starter, and Pro plans
planComparison.body:
DisputeDesk offers three plans:

Free ($0/month):
- 3 evidence packs per month.
- Manual pack generation only.
- PDF export.
- Save evidence to Shopify.

Starter ($29/month):
- 50 evidence packs per month.
- Auto-pack on dispute sync.
- Custom routing rules.
- PDF export and save to Shopify.
- 7-day free trial.

Pro ($79/month):
- Unlimited evidence packs.
- Auto-pack on dispute sync.
- Custom routing rules.
- Priority support.
- PDF export and save to Shopify.
- 7-day free trial.

All plans include the core features: evidence collection, completeness scoring, PDF export, and saving to Shopify. Paid plans add automation, rules, and higher quotas.

upgradingPlan.title: How to upgrade your plan
upgradingPlan.body:
To upgrade your DisputeDesk plan:

1. Go to the Billing page.
2. Review the plan comparison table.
3. Click "Upgrade to [Plan]" on the plan you want.
4. You'll be redirected to Shopify to approve the recurring charge.
5. After approval, your plan is activated immediately.

Paid plans include a 7-day free trial. You won't be charged until the trial period ends.

If you need to downgrade, contact support. Downgrades take effect at the end of your current billing cycle, and your data is always retained.

Your plan determines your monthly pack quota and which features are available (auto-pack, custom rules, priority support).

**From the marketing site:** Buttons on the public pricing section link to Billing with `?plan=…` so the right tier is selected or the upgrade flow starts. Open DisputeDesk from **Shopify Admin → Apps → DisputeDesk** so your store session is valid; if you are not in the embedded app, you may be prompted to open it from Admin first.

packLimits.title: Understanding pack limits and quotas
packLimits.body:
Each plan has a monthly limit on evidence packs:

- Free: 3 packs per month.
- Starter: 50 packs per month.
- Pro: Unlimited.

The counter resets on the first of each month. You can check your current usage on the Billing page under "Usage This Month."

When you reach your limit:
- New pack generation (manual or automatic) will be blocked.
- A warning banner will appear on the dispute detail page.
- You'll see an "Upgrade Plan" button to increase your quota.

Existing packs are not affected — you can still view, download PDFs, and save completed packs to Shopify even after hitting your limit.

trialPeriod.title: Free trial details
trialPeriod.body:
Both the Starter and Pro plans include a 7-day free trial.

During the trial:
- You have full access to all features of the plan.
- Your pack quota matches the plan level.
- No charge is applied until the trial ends.

After the trial:
- If you keep the plan, billing starts automatically through Shopify.
- If you cancel before the trial ends, you return to the Free plan with no charge.

Trials are managed through Shopify's billing system. You can view your billing status in Shopify Admin > Settings > Billing.

storeSessionUpgrade.title: Can't upgrade: "Store session is invalid"
storeSessionUpgrade.body:
If you see an error like "Store session is invalid (missing shop domain)" or "Reconnect this store to upgrade" when you try to change your plan, DisputeDesk doesn't have a valid connection to your Shopify store for billing.

To fix it:
1. In the sidebar, click **Clear shop & reconnect**.
2. Reconnect your store (enter your store domain and complete the Shopify authorization).
3. Open DisputeDesk from **Shopify Admin** (Apps → DisputeDesk) so the app runs with a valid store session.

The error message on the Billing page includes an **Open in Shopify Admin** link — use it to open your admin and launch the app from there. After that, try upgrading again from the Billing page.

howEvidenceSaved.title: How evidence is saved to Shopify
howEvidenceSaved.body:
When you save evidence, DisputeDesk pushes structured data to Shopify using the disputeEvidenceUpdate GraphQL API.

What gets saved (as text):
- Shipping and tracking documentation (carrier, tracking number, delivery status).
- Customer communication and order details.
- Refund and cancellation policy text.

What gets saved (as secure links):
- Each file you uploaded to the pack is included as a DisputeDesk link (https://disputedesk.app/e/...) inside the evidence text. Shopify's API does not let third-party apps attach files to a dispute, so the reviewer at the card issuer clicks the link and the file is served from our domain.
- The full evidence pack PDF is linked the same way.
- Links expire 180 days after the save, which covers the bank's review window.

Each section of your evidence pack is mapped to the appropriate Shopify evidence field. DisputeDesk handles the formatting and field mapping automatically.

After saving:
- The pack status changes to "Saved to Shopify."
- A deep link to Shopify Admin appears so you can review the evidence there.
- An audit event is logged for compliance tracking.

Important: saving evidence to Shopify is NOT the same as submitting to the card network. See "What happens after saving" for next steps.

fieldMapping.title: How evidence fields are mapped to Shopify
fieldMapping.body:
DisputeDesk maps pack content onto Shopify dispute evidence using the disputeEvidenceUpdate API:

- Fulfillment & delivery narrative — carrier wording, timelines, tracking text (from your pack/order) blends into Shopify's allowed text fields plus the broader rebuttal and activity narratives.
- Refund Policy → refundPolicyDisclosure.
- Cancellation Policy → cancellationPolicyDisclosure.
- Order facts & structured customer fields → accessActivityLog and the customer name/email fields Shopify accepts.

Uploaded files:
When the file evidence layer is enabled, DisputeDesk uploads a focused PDF per applicable native slot — Shipping documentation, Customer communication, Service documentation (Proof of service), and Other evidence (uncategorized) — so Shopify Admin's Chargeback response screen displays a populated row with a download icon. The PDF is generated by DisputeDesk and includes the reason the file is included plus key facts extracted from your pack (carrier, tracking, dates, policy acceptance timestamps). Your original uploaded file also remains as a labelled secure link inside the evidence text, so the issuer sees both the contextual summary and the source document.

Reason-aware slots: the Refund policy and Cancellation policy native rows render only on certain dispute reasons (refund/subscription cases). DisputeDesk currently keeps these as labelled links across every reason family until the rendering behaviour has been verified per family in Shopify Admin — narrowing later, never widening speculatively. When the file evidence layer is disabled, every file flows as a labelled link only and Shopify's native file rows remain empty.

Shipping details panel:
The shipping address and + Add tracking area come from Shopify order/fulfillment data. Uploading paperwork in DisputeDesk does not by itself populate tracking rows there unless that tracking exists on the fulfillment in Shopify.

Saving is automatic for mapping; submission to the issuer is handled by Shopify after you save or submit in Admin.

afterSaving.title: What happens after saving evidence
afterSaving.body:
After DisputeDesk saves your evidence to Shopify, here's what happens next:

1. Evidence appears in Shopify Admin: go to Orders > the linked order > Chargeback to review the evidence Shopify received.
2. Review in Shopify: you can add final notes or make adjustments directly in Shopify Admin.
3. Shopify sends evidence to the card network (Visa, Mastercard, etc.) either:
   - When you click the respond button in Shopify Admin, or
   - Automatically on the dispute's due date if you haven't responded manually.
4. Card network reviews: the card network evaluates the evidence and makes a decision.
5. Resolution: the dispute is resolved as "Won" (reversed in your favor) or "Lost."

DisputeDesk monitors the dispute status and updates it when Shopify reports a resolution.

**File evidence rows in Shopify Admin:** when the file evidence layer is enabled, **Shipping documentation**, **Customer communication**, **Proof of service**, and **Any other evidence** rows render a populated file with a download icon — DisputeDesk uploads a focused per-slot PDF that includes the reason and the key facts from your pack. Your original uploaded files also remain as labelled secure links (https://disputedesk.app/e/…) inside the evidence text, so the issuer has access to both the contextual summary and the source bytes. **Refund policy** and **Cancellation policy** rows are reason-aware — they only render on certain dispute reasons in Admin and are currently delivered as labelled links across all reason types. When the file evidence layer is disabled, every file flows as a labelled link only and Shopify's native file rows stay empty. Use **Review & Submit** here to preview the exact payload.

notSubmitToNetworks.title: DisputeDesk does NOT send evidence to card networks
notSubmitToNetworks.body:
This is an important distinction: DisputeDesk saves evidence to Shopify, but does NOT send it onward to card networks (Visa, Mastercard, American Express, etc.).

Here's the process:
1. DisputeDesk builds your evidence pack and saves it to Shopify via API.
2. Forwarding evidence to the card network is handled entirely by Shopify.
3. Shopify either auto-sends on the due date or you respond manually from Shopify Admin.

Why it works this way:
- Shopify is the merchant of record and handles the official communication with card networks.
- This ensures compliance with payment processor requirements.
- Your evidence is formatted and structured by DisputeDesk, then handed off to Shopify for the official process.

You always maintain control. Review your evidence in Shopify Admin before Shopify forwards it to the card network.

packVariables.title: Understanding pack variables
packVariables.body:
Pack variables are placeholders that automatically populate with order-specific data when DisputeDesk builds an evidence pack. They keep packs reusable while still producing fully personalized rebuttals.

**Common variables**
- `{{order.number}}` — the Shopify order number (e.g. `#1042`)
- `{{order.total}}` — order total formatted in the shop currency
- `{{order.created_at}}` — checkout timestamp
- `{{customer.name}}` — buyer first + last name
- `{{customer.email}}` — buyer email at checkout
- `{{tracking.number}}` — carrier tracking number when present
- `{{tracking.url}}` — direct link to the carrier status page
- `{{shipping.carrier}}` — carrier name (USPS, UPS, etc.)
- `{{policy.shipping}}`, `{{policy.refund}}`, `{{policy.terms}}` — your store policies

**Where they are used**
- Pack section narratives — DisputeDesk inserts the value when the pack is built.
- Defense letter and rebuttal — the AI uses variables to ground the narrative in real order data instead of generic templates.
- Manual edits — you can use the same `{{...}}` syntax in any text field.

**Tips**
- If a variable value is missing (e.g. no tracking number), DisputeDesk silently omits the surrounding sentence rather than printing an empty placeholder.
- Variables are case-sensitive: use `{{order.number}}`, not `{{Order.Number}}`.
- Test by opening any pack — DisputeDesk shows the resolved values in the preview before saving to Shopify.

packBestPractices.title: Evidence pack best practices
packBestPractices.body:
Winning a dispute is about giving the issuer enough decisive evidence to move the needle. Here is what works:

**1. Always include tracking with proof of delivery.** For Product Not Received claims, tracking that shows delivery — ideally with a signature — is the single highest-impact piece of evidence.

**2. Include AVS + CVV match for fraud claims.** Both must match. AVS-only or CVV-only is moderate; both together is strong.

**3. Reference your policies with timestamps.** Link the buyer checkout timestamp to the policy version they accepted. "Customer agreed to refund policy at 14:32 UTC on Mar 4" is decisive; "refund policy is on our website" is not.

**4. Show prior undisputed orders.** A history of successful purchases by the same customer/card/email weakens fraud claims significantly.

**5. Include explicit customer communication when available.** Emails, chat transcripts, or order notes where the buyer confirms delivery, use, or satisfaction are decisive.

**6. Show digital access for digital goods.** Login timestamps, download events, or feature usage are strong evidence the customer received the product.

**7. Avoid emotional language.** Stick to facts. "The buyer received the goods on Mar 5 (signature on file)" beats "the buyer is clearly trying to defraud us."

**8. Do not rely on collected ≠ strong.** A green collected badge means the field was filled in, not that the issuer will find it persuasive. Check the strength badge before submitting — see Evidence strength rubric.

**9. Keep narratives under 1 page.** Issuers spend seconds per case. Lead with the strongest 2-3 facts and the rebuttal.

**10. Watch your win rate.** DisputeDesk surfaces win rate by reason and family. If a category is consistently losing, look at what evidence is collected vs. submitted and adjust the playbook.

policyTypesExplained.title: Policy types: shipping, refund, terms, privacy
policyTypesExplained.body:
DisputeDesk treats policies as first-class evidence. Each policy type strengthens a different category of dispute.

**Shipping policy**
What to include: delivery timeframes (e.g. 3-5 business days domestic), carrier list, tracking commitment, international handling, lost-package process.
When it strengthens evidence: Product Not Received, late delivery, wrong-address claims. Pair with the carrier tracking proof.

**Refund policy**
What to include: return window (e.g. 30 days), refund timeline, restocking fees, conditions (unopened, original packaging), exclusions (final-sale, perishables).
When it strengthens evidence: refund not processed, subscription cancellations, buyer-remorse claims framed as fraud. Issuers want to see the customer agreed to specific terms with a timestamp.

**Terms of service**
What to include: account terms, acceptable use, dispute resolution clause, governing law.
When it strengthens evidence: subscription disputes, digital-goods claims ("I didn't agree to this"), recurring charges. The terms link the customer to the relationship.

**Privacy policy**
What to include: data collection scope, retention, third-party sharing, customer rights (access, deletion).
When it strengthens evidence: rarely used in chargeback evidence directly, but referenced when the dispute touches account access or unauthorized-use claims.

**Tip**
DisputeDesk uses the policy text — not just a link — to build evidence. Upload the actual policy (TXT, Markdown, or the link plus a snapshot) so the AI can quote the relevant clause in the rebuttal.

policyVariables.title: Using policy variables in packs
policyVariables.body:
Reference your store policies in evidence pack narratives using policy variables. DisputeDesk inserts the policy text (or a clickable link) automatically when the pack is built.

**Available variables**
- `{{policy.shipping}}` — your shipping policy
- `{{policy.refund}}` — your refund / return policy
- `{{policy.terms}}` — your terms of service
- `{{policy.privacy}}` — your privacy policy

**How it works**
When DisputeDesk builds a pack and encounters a policy variable, it pulls from the policies you uploaded in Settings → Policies. If you uploaded a TXT or Markdown file, the variable resolves to the relevant excerpt. If you only uploaded a URL, the variable resolves to a clickable link.

**Example**
In a pack narrative for a Product Not Received dispute:

> As stated in our shipping policy, all orders are delivered within 3-5 business days with tracking. The customer accepted these terms at checkout on `{{order.created_at}}`. Tracking confirms delivery on Mar 5 — see `{{tracking.url}}`.

**Tips**
- Pair `{{policy.refund}}` with `{{order.created_at}}` to anchor the policy to the buyer checkout timestamp. Issuers find this far more compelling than a generic "see our policy" line.
- If a policy is not uploaded, the variable silently omits the surrounding sentence — do not reference policies you have not uploaded yet.
- Update policies in Settings → Policies and DisputeDesk uses the new text on the next pack build. No need to edit each pack.

policyBestPractices.title: Policy best practices that win disputes
policyBestPractices.body:
Strong policies, anchored to the buyer checkout timestamp, are some of the most decisive evidence available. Here is how to make yours stand out.

**1. Upload the actual policy text — not just a link.** A live URL can change. A TXT or Markdown file uploaded to DisputeDesk preserves the exact version the buyer accepted at checkout. Issuers want to see the version, not the current site.

**2. Timestamp every policy.** When you update a policy, version it. "Refund Policy v3 — effective Mar 1" lets the rebuttal say "the customer accepted v3 at checkout on Mar 5."

**3. Be specific about timeframes.** "Refunds processed within 5 business days of return receipt" beats "refunds are processed promptly." Specificity reads as a real commitment, not boilerplate.

**4. Include explicit checkout consent.** Show a checkbox in your checkout flow that says "I agree to the refund policy" with the timestamp. This is the single strongest policy evidence available.

**5. Cover the predictable failure modes.** Lost in transit, late delivery, wrong address, refund timing, subscription cancellation, digital-goods access. If your policy is silent on the dispute reason, the issuer reads silence as ambiguity.

**6. Match policy language to the dispute reason.** Shipping policy → Product Not Received. Refund policy → Credit Not Processed. Terms → Subscription Canceled. DisputeDesk auto-selects the right policy variable based on the dispute family.

**7. Do not hide policies behind a click.** Policies linked in tiny footer text are weaker than policies shown at checkout. Issuers know the difference.

**8. Keep them readable.** Plain English wins. Legal-jargon policies are technically valid but harder to quote in a rebuttal.

**9. Update policies at least annually.** Stale policies (last updated 2019) are less convincing than current ones.

**10. Test the variables.** After uploading a policy, build a test pack and confirm the variable resolves correctly in the preview.

understandingInquiries.title: Understanding Inquiries
understandingInquiries.body:
An inquiry is the first stage of a dispute — before it becomes a formal chargeback.

What happens during an inquiry:
- The customer's bank contacts Shopify with questions about a transaction.
- This is NOT yet a chargeback. No funds have been reversed.
- You have an opportunity to respond with information that may resolve the issue.

Why inquiries matter:
- Responding promptly to an inquiry can prevent it from escalating to a chargeback.
- A well-prepared response at this stage saves time, money, and effort.
- DisputeDesk identifies inquiries and helps you prepare the right response.

How DisputeDesk handles inquiries:
- Inquiries appear in your disputes list with an 'Inquiry' badge.
- The dispute detail page uses inquiry-specific language and CTAs.
- Automation and playbooks can be configured for inquiry-specific handling.

Key difference from chargebacks:
- Inquiries are informational — the bank is asking questions.
- Chargebacks are formal — funds are reversed and you must submit evidence.

understandingChargebacks.title: Understanding Chargebacks
understandingChargebacks.body:
A chargeback is a formal dispute where the customer's bank has reversed the transaction.

What happens during a chargeback:
- The bank reverses the funds from the merchant's account.
- You have a limited window (usually 7-21 days) to submit evidence.
- If you don't respond, you lose the dispute automatically.

How DisputeDesk handles chargebacks:
- Chargebacks appear with a 'Chargeback' badge and stronger urgency.
- DisputeDesk automatically builds evidence packs using order data, tracking info, and customer communications.
- Evidence is saved to Shopify, where it's forwarded to the card network.

Evidence that helps win chargebacks:
- Proof of delivery (tracking numbers, delivery confirmation)
- Order confirmation and customer communication
- Store policies (refund, shipping, terms of service)
- Fraud screening data (AVS match, CVV verification)

Timelines are critical. DisputeDesk monitors deadlines and ensures evidence is prepared well before the due date.

lifecycleOverview.title: How DisputeDesk Handles the Dispute Lifecycle
lifecycleOverview.body:
Every dispute goes through a lifecycle with two main phases: Inquiry and Chargeback.

Phase 1 — Inquiry:
- The bank asks questions about a transaction.
- No funds reversed yet.
- Prompt response can prevent escalation.
- DisputeDesk labels these as 'Inquiry' throughout the app.

Phase 2 — Chargeback:
- The bank formally reverses funds.
- Evidence submission required within a deadline.
- DisputeDesk labels these as 'Chargeback' with stronger urgency.

How coverage works across phases:
- Each dispute family (Fraud, Product Not Received, etc.) can have different handling for inquiries vs chargebacks.
- The Coverage page shows how each family is handled in both phases.
- Automation rules currently apply to both phases equally.

What you should do:
1. Check your Coverage page to see which families are protected.
2. Review your Automation settings for each dispute type.
3. Install playbooks for the dispute types most relevant to your store.
4. Monitor the Dashboard for inquiry and chargeback queue counts.

ce30Overview.title: Visa Compelling Evidence 3.0 — what it is and when it qualifies
ce30Overview.body:
Visa Compelling Evidence 3.0 (CE 3.0) is Visa's program that shifts the liability for a chargeback back to the issuing bank when a merchant can prove that the same cardholder made earlier legitimate purchases. It applies only to Visa disputes filed under reason code 10.4 (Other Fraud — Card-Absent Environment).

When CE 3.0 applies, the dispute is harder for the issuer to win — Visa expects the issuer to accept the evidence and reverse the chargeback.

Qualification rules:
1. The cardholder has at least 2 prior undisputed transactions with your store.
2. Those transactions happened between 120 and 365 days before the disputed transaction.
3. At least 2 of these data points match across all three transactions (disputed + 2 priors): IP address, device fingerprint, shipping address, customer account ID.
4. At least one of those matches must be IP or device — this is called the 'anchor' requirement.

The DisputeDesk Liability-Shift panel on each dispute tells you the verdict immediately: Qualifies / Qualifies (low confidence) / Partial / Does not qualify / Not applicable. When a dispute qualifies, DisputeDesk generates a CE 3.0-formatted evidence package and attaches it to the Shopify dispute response.

Guest checkouts can still qualify, but with lower confidence — DisputeDesk matches on email instead of customer ID. B2B / commercial cards qualify just like consumer cards.

What CE 3.0 does NOT cover: anything other than Visa reason code 10.4. For 'product not received', 'not as described', or other non-fraud reasons, your standard evidence pack still applies.

autoQualificationVisaSecure.title: Auto-qualification via Visa Secure — and the April 2026 fee
autoQualificationVisaSecure.body:
Effective October 17, 2025, Visa automatically pre-qualifies for CE 3.0 any transaction authenticated via Visa Secure (3-D Secure 2) or Visa Data Only (frictionless 3DS data exchange). When this auto-qualification fires, the dispute is pre-qualified at the Visa network level — you don't need 2 prior transactions or matching data points.

DisputeDesk detects this automatically by reading the 3-D Secure state on the disputed order. The Liability-Shift panel shows 'Pre-qualified by Visa' with a green badge.

What you still need to do: submit your rebuttal evidence as normal. The auto-qualification is metadata attached at Visa's end — your evidence is what completes the defense.

April 17, 2026 — Visa is introducing a fee:
Visa will start charging a per-qualification fee on every successful auto-qualification, billed through your acquirer. DisputeDesk surfaces a notice in the Liability-Shift panel whenever this applies (i.e., for any disputed transaction created on or after April 17, 2026 that qualifies via Visa Secure).

This is automatic and there is no opt-in or opt-out — you simply receive the benefit and the associated fee shows up on your acquirer statement. Talk to your payment processor if you need fee specifics for your account.

Mastercard 3DS does NOT auto-qualify for CE 3.0 — CE 3.0 is Visa-only. Mastercard first-party-fraud disputes follow the separate FPT path (see 'Mastercard FPT' help article).

subscriptionCe30.title: How subscription / recurring billing qualifies for CE 3.0
subscriptionCe30.body:
Visa CE 3.0 has a special path for recurring or merchant-initiated transactions (MIT). For a subscription customer, the IP address and device fingerprint usually differ between bills — the customer signed up once and got charged monthly. Visa recognizes this and allows the merchant to use the initial subscription billing transaction (the original signup) as the matching anchor, instead of looking at 120–365-day-old priors.

DisputeDesk detects subscription orders automatically. It recognizes:
- Native Shopify Subscriptions (line items with a selling plan)
- Common third-party apps (Recharge, Bold, Loop, Skio, Appstle)
- Orders tagged 'subscription' or 'recurring'

When a subscription dispute lands, DisputeDesk looks up the initial billing transaction and matches IP / device / shipping / account across the disputed bill and the initial billing. If 2 data points match (with at least one being IP or device), the verdict is 'Qualifies via initial billing'.

Edge cases:
- First-bill dispute (the customer disputed the signup itself, not a recurring bill) → no initial billing exists yet, so DisputeDesk falls back to the standard CE 3.0 path (looking for 120–365-day-old priors).
- Initial billing was refunded or disputed → excluded; falls back to the standard path.
- Recurring transactions never match each other on IP/device anyway → the initial-billing path is the right approach.

This branch is generally medium-confidence (never 'high') because it matches against only one prior transaction. The package DisputeDesk generates explains this clearly to the issuer.

mastercardFpt.title: Mastercard First-Party Trust (FPT)
mastercardFpt.body:
Mastercard First-Party Trust is the Mastercard equivalent of Visa CE 3.0 — but it works differently. FPT applies to Mastercard first-party-fraud disputes (the cardholder claims they didn't authorize the transaction or doesn't recognize it). The eligible reason codes are 4837 (No Cardholder Authorization) and 4863 (Cardholder Does Not Recognize).

FPT does NOT require prior transactions. Instead, it asks whether you have strong evidence across three categories:
- Device: IP address, device fingerprint, 3-D Secure authentication, session behavior
- Delivery: shipping address, tracking, delivery confirmation, signed-by-name
- Identity: customer account, account tenure, login state at checkout, repeat-customer status

DisputeDesk scores each category 0–1 and a dispute is 'ready' for FPT when all three categories have evidence AND the total score is at least 2.0 out of 3.0.

Regional availability is important. FPT is live in:
- United States — since October 2024
- Canada, LATAM (including Brazil), Caribbean, APAC — since June 2025
- European Union — not yet available

If your store is in a region where FPT isn't live, DisputeDesk shows 'Not applicable' on the Liability-Shift panel and falls back to standard Mastercard representment.

Important operational note: DisputeDesk generates an FPT-formatted package and submits it through the Shopify dispute API as best-effort. Direct submission to Mastercard's Ethoca Consumer Clarity API requires a separate commercial partnership that DisputeDesk is pursuing but doesn't have yet.

networkReasonCodes.title: Network reason codes — Visa and Mastercard, not Shopify
networkReasonCodes.body:
Shopify groups all disputes into 14 broad categories (Fraudulent, Product Not Received, Subscription Canceled, etc.). But Visa and Mastercard use much more specific reason codes underneath: Visa 10.4, 13.1, 13.3, Mastercard 4837, 4855, and so on. The specific network code is what determines how the issuing bank evaluates your evidence and what kind of rebuttal language wins.

DisputeDesk resolves the underlying network reason code automatically for every dispute. The resolution uses several signals (in order of reliability):
- Direct: a typed field on the Shopify dispute (currently not exposed by Shopify, so this is reserved for a future API change)
- Derived: parsed from the payment gateway's transaction receipt when available (Shopify Payments only)
- Inferred: best-guess mapping from Shopify's enum + the card network + order context
- Unknown: signal not available; standard handling applies

The dispute detail page shows the resolved code (e.g., 'Visa 13.1 — Merchandise/Services Not Received') with a confidence indicator. Confident resolution lets DisputeDesk:
1. Detect CE 3.0 eligibility (Visa 10.4 → CE 3.0 path)
2. Detect FPT eligibility (Mastercard 4837 / 4863 → FPT path)
3. Pick more specific rebuttal templates per code (Visa 13.1, 13.2, and 13.3 each get different language even though they all map to 'Product Not Received' in Shopify's enum)
4. Apply tailored evidence checklists per code

You don't need to do anything — resolution is automatic. If a code resolves as 'unknown', DisputeDesk falls back gracefully to the standard handling for the Shopify enum value.

vampRatioExplained.title: VAMP, ECM, and EFM — what the numbers mean
vampRatioExplained.body:
Card networks monitor three key chargeback ratios for every merchant. Crossing the thresholds triggers fees, enrollment in monitoring programs, and in extreme cases account termination. The DisputeDesk Ratio Dashboard shows your calculated estimates plus the counterfactual impact of DisputeDesk's wins.

The three ratios:
- Visa VAMP (Acquirer Monitoring Program) — total disputes / total settled transactions. Standard threshold: 0.65%. Excessive threshold: 1.50%. Crossing excessive triggers a per-transaction enforcement fee.
- Mastercard ECM (Excessive Chargeback Merchant) — Mastercard chargebacks / Mastercard settled. Threshold: 1.00%.
- Mastercard EFM (Excessive Fraud Merchant) — Mastercard fraud chargebacks / Mastercard settled. Threshold: 0.50%.

DisputeDesk shows a yellow warning at 80% of each threshold and a red alert when you cross it. We also email you when bands change.

The counterfactual line is the key insight: DisputeDesk-attributed wins (CE 3.0 and FPT successes) are removed from your VAMP numerator when calculating your ratio. The dashed line shows what your ratio would be without DisputeDesk's work — the gap between the two lines is the value DisputeDesk delivered.

Important caveat: these are calculated estimates from your Shopify data, not the official numbers your acquirer reports. Only your acquirer has the authoritative ratio. DisputeDesk's calculation uses the standard formula but approximates TC40 / TC15 / TC05 settlement codes from Shopify's dispute and order data. If your acquirer's number differs, theirs is the one that matters for compliance — ours is a working approximation to spot trends early.

Monthly impact summary on the dashboard shows: disputes qualified, wins by channel, transactions removed from VAMP, estimated fees avoided, and estimated revenue recovered.

sessionCapture.title: Storefront session capture — what it is and what we store
sessionCapture.body:
To match disputes against CE 3.0 / FPT requirements, DisputeDesk needs to know certain facts about each customer's checkout session: what IP address they used, whether they were logged in, the pages they viewed, the device they used. Without this data, qualification rates stay artificially low — most disputes will fall short of the matching-data-point requirement.

What DisputeDesk captures (when storefront session capture is enabled):
- The Shopify cart_token (so we can match the session to the eventual order)
- IP address (hashed at rest with a per-shop salt; raw value encrypted and decrypted only at qualification time)
- IP-derived geography (country and region only, never city or precise location)
- User agent string
- Customer ID and login state at checkout (if logged in)
- Customer account age (e.g., 'this customer joined 200 days ago')
- Pages viewed during the session and time spent on the checkout page
- Privacy signals from the browser (Do Not Track, Global Privacy Control)

What DisputeDesk does NOT capture:
- Form input values (names, addresses, card numbers, anything typed)
- Composite device fingerprints (canvas / WebGL / audio fingerprinting is deferred to a later, legal-reviewed phase)
- Mouse movement or behavioral entropy
- Cross-session cookies linking your storefront to other sites

Privacy controls:
- Do Not Track and Global Privacy Control signals cause DisputeDesk to drop the session record server-side
- Session data is automatically deleted 18 months after capture (covers the 365-day CE 3.0 window plus buffer)
- LGPD / GDPR / CCPA right-to-be-forgotten requests are honored via the merchant-facing subject-deletion endpoint
- DisputeDesk acts as your data processor; you are the controller

You'll need to update your storefront's privacy policy to disclose this capture. DisputeDesk provides a template you can adapt.

Forward-looking note: session capture doesn't help disputes filed before you enable it (we have no data on those sessions). It builds the evidence base for every dispute filed after install.

understandingDashboard.title: Understanding the dashboard in this app
understandingDashboard.body:
The dashboard gives you an at-a-glance view of your dispute operations and lets you control automation from one place.

**KPI cards**
Four metrics at the top update based on the selected time period (24h / 7d / 30d / All):
- **Active Disputes** — disputes currently open and awaiting a response or under review.
- **Win Rate** — percentage of resolved disputes you won (Won divided by Won + Lost).
- **Evidence Packs** — total evidence packs created for your store.
- **Amount at Risk** — total disputed amount across all currently active disputes.

Where a previous period exists, each card shows a percentage change (green arrow = improved, red arrow = declined).

**Automation Status card**
Shows the four pipeline controls for your store:

- **Auto Build** (ON/OFF) — when a new dispute syncs from Shopify, DisputeDesk automatically creates an evidence pack and starts collecting evidence (order data, tracking info, store policies). If OFF, you click Generate Pack manually on each dispute.

- **Auto Save** (ON/OFF) — once a pack is built and passes the completeness threshold, DisputeDesk automatically saves it to Shopify so it is attached to the dispute. If OFF, you review the pack first and click Save to Shopify manually.

- **Min Score** — the completeness percentage a pack must reach before Auto Save fires. A pack below this score waits until more evidence is collected. You can still save manually below the threshold with a confirmation prompt.

- **Blocker Gate** (ON/OFF) — packs can have blockers: missing critical evidence such as a signed delivery confirmation or a required policy document. When ON, Auto Save is additionally blocked if any blocker is unresolved, regardless of the completeness score. Even a 95% complete pack will not auto-save while a blocker remains.

**Example:** Auto Build ON, Auto Save OFF, Min Score 80%, Blocker Gate ON — DisputeDesk collects evidence automatically for every new dispute, but you review and save each pack manually before it goes to Shopify.

**Recent Disputes table**
Lists your five latest chargebacks. Click the order number to jump directly to that order in Shopify Admin, or click View Details to open the dispute and manage its evidence pack.

afterSaving.title: What happens after saving evidence
afterSaving.body:
After you save evidence from this app to Shopify:

1. Evidence appears in Shopify Admin: go to Orders → the linked order → Chargeback to review what Shopify received.
2. Review in Shopify: you can add final notes or make adjustments in Shopify Admin.
3. Shopify sends evidence to the card network when you click respond in Shopify Admin, or automatically on the dispute's due date.
4. The card network reviews and resolves the dispute as Won or Lost.

DisputeDesk updates the dispute status when Shopify reports the resolution.

**File rows in Shopify Admin:** when file evidence attachments are enabled, **Shipping documentation**, **Customer communication**, **Proof of service**, and **Any other evidence** rows render a populated file with a download icon — DisputeDesk uploads a focused PDF per slot that includes the reason and key facts from your pack. Your original uploaded files also remain as labelled secure links (https://disputedesk.app/e/…) in the evidence text. **Refund policy** and **Cancellation policy** rows only render on certain dispute reasons; until that's verified per family, those files flow as labelled links. When the layer is disabled, every file flows as a labelled link only. Use **Review & Submit** here to preview the exact payload.

viewingFilteringDisputes.title: Viewing and filtering disputes
viewingFilteringDisputes.body:
The **Disputes** page uses Polaris **Page** with a toolbar and a table inside **Card**. The toolbar has **Search** (dispute ID, order, reason, or customer name), **Filter** (status popover), **Export** (CSV download), and **More actions** ⋯ for **Sync now**.

The table matches the dashboard **Recent Disputes** columns: **Order** (links to Shopify Admin when available), **ID** (short id), **Customer**, **Amount**, **Reason**, **Status** (badge), **Deadline**, and **Actions** with **View details** to open the dispute. The order link opens Shopify Admin without leaving the list.

There is no separate **Review Queue** tab. Use **Approve & Save** on the detail page when ready.

disputeDetailPage.title: Dispute detail in this app
disputeDetailPage.body:
From **Disputes**, choose **View details** to open this page.

- **KPIs**: amount, status, due date, time left (urgent styling when the deadline is close or past).
- **Dispute status**: five steps from Created through Outcome. The rail advances as packs exist and evidence is **saved to Shopify** (manual save or automation). Terminal outcomes mark all steps complete.
- **Supplemental evidence** unlocks after a save to Shopify — then **Open evidence pack** goes to the pack where you upload extra files.
- **Timeline** mixes Shopify order events with DisputeDesk milestones.
- **Evidence packs** lists every pack for the dispute.

Actions: **Generate Pack**, **Re-sync**, and **Open dispute in Shopify** when the link is available. Locale in the URL refetches profile data so timeline text can follow the store language when Shopify returns localized events.

reviewQueue.title: The review queue
reviewQueue.body:
The review queue is disputes your rules route to **manual review** before evidence is saved to Shopify.

Disputes land here when:
- A rule sends them to review (for example high value).
- No rule matches and the default is review.
- **Require review before auto-save** is on in automation settings.

In the embedded app, those disputes appear on the **Disputes** list with your other chargebacks — use **Filter** by status or open items from the dashboard. Open a dispute to inspect the pack, then use **Approve & Save** on the detail page when ready.

This keeps automation for simple cases and hands unusual or sensitive disputes to you.

approvingDisputes.title: Approving disputes from the review queue
approvingDisputes.body:
Approve from the **dispute detail** page after you open a dispute from the list or dashboard.

Steps:
1. Go to **Disputes** and choose **View details** (or open the dispute from the dashboard).
2. Review the evidence pack and completeness on the detail page.
3. Use **Approve & Save** to run the pipeline and save evidence to Shopify when your gates pass.

You can generate or refresh packs on the detail page first. There is no **Approve** button only on the list — the detail page is where you confirm evidence before saving.
